findings.finding: The plan specifies that `set_baseline` will 'never write `baseline_advanced_at`' but does not require removing the key from entries that already have it in the existing `bindings.json`. The RETIRE path covers stopping new writes but not evicting the field from existing data. Any entry that already has `baseline_advanced_at` written will silently retain it until a migration or an explicit `entry.pop('baseline_advanced_at', None)` in `set_baseline` removes it. The grep AC (`grep -rn baseline_advanced_at src/`) checks source code only and would pass even if every existing entry still carries the field in the data file. The byte-identity AC would also pass (two post-implementation passes both leave old entries unchanged), masking the data-level leak.
findings.location: ## Approach — 'never write `baseline_advanced_at`'; ## Acceptance Criteria — grep AC and byte-identity AC
scenarios: After A1 ships, any bindings.json entry that was last touched before the release retains baseline_advanced_at indefinitely; a downstream consumer or audit that inspects the data file (not src/) still sees the field, contradicting the plan's stated goal of deleting it.
The packed-cost measurement for entries not subsequently updated by set_baseline still reflects the old field presence, potentially understating post-implementation savings for long-lived entries.
findings.suggested_fix: In `set_baseline`, after constructing the filtered baseline and before the equality guard, add `entry.pop('baseline_advanced_at', None)`. This ensures the field is evicted from any pre-existing entry on its next touch without requiring a separate migration pass. Add a unit AC: 'An entry loaded from a legacy bindings.json containing baseline_advanced_at no longer has the key after set_baseline is called on it.'
